In rural health facilities in Bangladesh, the effect of the intervention on the number of children receiving BCG and Pentavalent vaccines in urban settings is uncertain due to the very low certainty of evidence. This assessment is based on a single non-randomized controlled trial (non-RCT). 2. In Ethiopia, the effect of the intervention on the number of women giving birth at healthcare facilities is uncertain because the certainty of the evidence was assessed as very low. This conclusion is derived from a single non-RCT conducted in both urban and rural health facilities. 3. Similarly, in Ethiopia, the effect of the intervention on the number of women attending at least four antenatal care visits is uncertain due to the very low certainty of evidence. This finding is based on a single non-RCT conducted in urban and rural health facilities. 4. The effect of the intervention on the number of women attending postnatal care at health centers in Ethiopia is also uncertain, as the certainty of the evidence was assessed as very low. This conclusion is based on a single non-RCT conducted in urban and rural health facilities. 5. No studies were identified that reported on the timeliness of receiving healthcare services. Therefore, the effect of the intervention on the time between presentation and appropriate management is uncertain due to the lack of direct evidence. 6. No studies were identified that reported on health status and well-being. Consequently, the effect of the intervention on health status and well-being is uncertain due to the absence of direct evidence. 7. No studies were identified that reported on providers' acceptability or satisfaction. As a result, the effect of the intervention on providers' acceptability or satisfaction is uncertain due to the lack of direct evidence. 8. Similarly, no studies were identified that reported on patient acceptability or satisfaction. Therefore, the effect of the intervention on patient acceptability or satisfaction is uncertain due to the absence of direct evidence. 9. No studies were identified that reported on the quality of data about services provided. Consequently, the effect of the intervention on the quality of data about services is uncertain due to the lack of direct evidence. 10. No studies were identified that reported on resource use. Thus, the effect of the intervention on resource use is uncertain due to the absence of direct evidence. 11. No studies were identified that reported on unintended consequences. Therefore, the effect of the intervention on unintended consequences is uncertain due to the lack of direct evidence. 12. Digital tracking with clinical decision support and targeted client communication (one-way information support) was compared to standard care without the use of digital aids. The intervention targeted nurses and health officers providing maternal and child health services to pregnant women, as well as health assistants and vaccinators providing vaccination services to children aged 0–11 months. The settings included primary health facilities in rural and urban Ethiopia and community-based settings in hard-to-reach rural and urban areas of Bangladesh. 13. Health workers in rural and remote areas particularly value the efficiency of digital health technologies, as these allow them to provide services more effectively. They also appreciate the portability of these technologies, which enables flexibility and reduces the need to be office-bound. 14. Some health workers report that digital health technologies enhance their social status and increase the trust and respect they receive from their communities. This is partly due to the use of advanced devices and their ability to access higher-level care. 15. However, some health workers do not find digital health interventions efficient, as they may increase their workload rather than reduce it. This can lead to lower acceptance of these interventions. 16. Health workers often face logistical challenges when using digital health technologies, such as poor network connectivity and limited access to electricity for charging devices. These issues are particularly prevalent in rural and remote areas. 17. Health workers require easy-to-use, reliable equipment and ongoing technical support. They also feel that these technologies could be expanded to a wider range of settings, services, and illnesses. 18. Poor integration of digital health interventions with existing systems and usability issues, such as language barriers and device limitations, can hinder their effectiveness and acceptance. 19. Training is considered essential for staff acceptance and effective use of digital health technologies. Health workers and trainers believe that familiarity with these technologies can help overcome initial difficulties. 20. Health workers may be concerned about the confidentiality of medical information and data security when using digital health devices, particularly for stigmatized conditions such as HIV/AIDS. Achieving informed consent for sharing records and images can also be challenging in settings with low literacy levels. 21. Health workers' perceptions of digital health interventions are influenced by their pre-existing technology literacy. Those who are more technologically competent tend to have positive views, while those who struggle with these technologies may have negative perceptions and feel anxious about making errors. 22. Even technologically proficient users often require ongoing support and repeated training to effectively use digital health programs and devices. 23. Rapid changes in technology and unmet expectations regarding digital health interventions can lead to dissatisfaction among health workers. 24. Some health workers express concerns about the personal costs associated with using their own mobile phones and internet access for work purposes. While some feel a moral obligation to assist clients despite these costs, others view these expenses as a burden.
